forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: North Kesteven projects £533k general fund surplus as borrowing costs fall
news_drafts.lead: North Kesteven Council is projecting a General Fund surplus of £533,300 for 2026-27, driven mainly by lower-than-expected borrowing costs. The council budgeted for £2.54m in interest payments but now expects to spend only £1.92m, a saving of £617,600 built on timing of planned loan drawdowns for Lafford Homes development that concentrate borrowing into the second half of the year. Pay awards 0.3 percentage points higher than budgeted cost £51,400, and additional fuel costs add £22,800 of pressure. The surplus is being added to reserves: £233,300 to the Our Council Reserve and £300,000 to the Financial Resilience Reserve. The Housing Revenue Account, by contrast, projects a deficit of £160,700. The council is also managing capital scheme underspending of £1.8m against a budget of £10.1m, suggesting capital projects are not progressing at the pace anticipated in February.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Key Performance Indicator Exception Report Quarter 1 2026/27

findings.headline: The five-year financial planning allows for unavoidable cost pressures, with the paper stating this as its policy on bids for growth and service investment.
findings.detail: The paper states that the policy on bids for growth and service investment is that the five-year financial planning allows for unavoidable cost pressures only. This sets the scope of what the MTFS will fund beyond existing commitments.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing councils' budget-setting policies will want to know whether discretionary growth bids are funded, since this determines how much headroom exists for new service pressures.
findings.quote: The five-year financial planning allows for unavoidable cost pressures only.

findings.headline: Government Revenue Support Grant is assumed at nil and New Homes Bonus has been revoked from 2025/26.
findings.detail: The paper's assumptions table records Government Grant for RSG as nil and states that New Homes Bonus was revoked in 2025/26. These two items are set out as the baseline for the 2027/28 strategy.
findings.matters: A council with no RSG and no New Homes Bonus depends more heavily on council tax, business rates and fees, which is a position other councils managing funding losses will compare against.

findings.headline: Renewable energy income from NNDR is assumed to rise from £3,739,600 in 2026/27 to £4,334,000 in 2031/32.
findings.detail: The paper sets out a forecast schedule of NNDR renewable energy income, with figures of £3,739,600 for 2026/27, £3,969,000 for 2027/28, £4,045,000 for 2028/29, £4,146,000 for 2029/30, £4,249,000 for 2030/31 and £4,334,000 for 2031/32.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council with renewable generation in its tax base will recognise the sensitivity of a single income stream to the assumed trajectory.

findings.headline: Our Environment Reserve contribution from the general fund is set at £1.1m for 2026/27, falling to £600k in 2027/28 and ceasing from 2031/32, funded by assumed grant income.
findings.detail: The paper states the contribution is currently £1.1m for 2026/27 and is to reduce to £600k in 2027/28, £450k in 2028/29, £300k in 2029/30 and £150k in 2030/31, ceasing from 2031/32. It notes that the reduction is funded by assumed grant income receivable.
findings.matters: The reserve's general fund contributions depend on grant income not yet confirmed, so the council's ability to sustain environment-related spending over the period rests on that assumption.

findings.headline: Employer pension contribution rates fall from 1 April 2026 following the October 2025 triennial review, with the secondary rate reduced to nil.
findings.detail: The paper says the triennial review was completed in October 2025 and that the primary rate decreased from 23.6% to 17.6% from 01/04/26. It states that the secondary rate was reduced by £416k to nil. The last triennial valuation applies for 2026/27 to 2028/29.
findings.matters: A lower employer contribution rate reduces a major establishment cost for the council, and other councils in the same pension fund cycle will be watching how the rate change feeds through their own budgets.
findings.quote: Primary Rate decreased from 23.6% to 17.6% effective 01/04/26. Secondary rate reduced £416k to £nil.
